catalog_quote: [Wilson 1986:287] All of the Wakashan languages distinguish between light and heavy syllables, that is, between non-branching and branching rimes. In Kwakiutlan, a light syllable contains a reduced vowel. A heavy syllable contains a full vowel (which may appear on the surface as either long or short), or a reduced vowel followed by a tautosyllabic sonorant that fills the second V-slot in the branching rime. The basic stress rule of Kwakwala places primary stress on the first heavy syllable in a word. Secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables after the primary stress. Epenthetic schwas, which are inserted after stress assignment, are therefore not counted in placing secondary stresses. ... Secondary stresses that would fall on reduced vowels are never marked in the data. ... [p.288] At this point, it is important to emphasize two features of the Kwakwala stress system. First, prim…
sweep_summary: search for kwak1269 (Kwak'wala, catalog classification weight, deciding source Wilson 1986 BLS 12:287-288) had a single title item: Bach 1975, 'Long vowels and stress in Kwakiutl', Texas Linguistic Forum 2:9-19, already in our bibliography. It is unambiguously about word stress in this language (Glottolog record 671236; Bach's own publication list and Northern Wakashan checklist, the Internet Archive copies saved). No open copy could be found: no DOI/record on Crossref, Semantic Scholar or OpenAlex; archive.org has other TLF volumes but not 1975; the the Internet Archive index of both of Bach's UMass sites shows only three unrelated PDFs; Google Books lists the 1975 TLF volume (id rPZhaRgAEusC, 186 pp.) with no view; HathiTrust, Google Books pages and WorldCat are bot-walled by automated download; Access = print only, priority high (it is the classic first-hand rule statement and the source every later description cites). Its rule is, however, quoted verbatim in the held Janzen 2015 thesis (p.44, scanned verified in this search of works with stress in the title): 'Stress first syllable with long vowel or vowel plus tautosyllabic resonant or if none stress last syllable', and Gordon 2000 and Werle 2010 (both held) transmit the same leftmost-heavy-else-final rule from Bach 1975; so as far as it can be read second-hand it confirms the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and does not supersede Wilson 1986. Nothing new was read first-hand, so no new stress statement was found; three bibliographic pages were and logged in there.
